newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Buy radios not warplanes, US tells NATO recruits.
newsitem.headline: Buy radios not warplanes, US tells NATO recruits.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday urged Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to spend funds on new radios and restructuring before buying fighter jets and other costly arms as they march into NATO.

Cohen spoke as he arrived in Hungary from a NATO summit in Madrid, where western leaders invited the three former Communist states to join the alliance in 1999 if they can meet strict financial and military requirements.
"I would say (spend) less on the more expensive equipment and focus on the command and control and communications," Cohen said in an interview with reporters travelling with him.
He said that establishing common communications with NATO armies was more important now for the new democracies than building arsenals with scarce military funds.
"English language training is also going to be very important and that is not an expensive proposition," he said.

Cohen will meet on Thursday with Hungary's President Arpad Goncz, Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti and parliamentary leaders on changes demanded by NATO for Hungary's Soviet-equipped military. He said most of that Soviet equipment must eventually be phased out.

Cohen said he told defence ministers of the three countries in an hour-long meeting in Madrid earlier on Monday that "we are happy to be in a celebratory mood, but now we have to get down to business."

"Now we get down to talking about what has to be done for the ratification process (by NATO members) to go through and dealing with the hard issues of restructuring their military, reforming it, forming an NCO (non-commissioned officers) corps, upgrading their facilities," the secretary said.

"They will spend less on defence by joining an alliance such as this and by rationalising their defence requirements rather than engaging in a race up the defence ladder to see who can buy more equipment and more expensive equipment to demonstrate their superiority."

It is a major task for new democracies with budget problems, ageing Soviet military equipment and the eventual prospect of buying billions of dollars in new arms in addition to such basics as establishing common communications and command and control links with NATO.

Cohen and other U.S. officials stressed he was not in Hungary to sell arms, although Budapest is shopping for some 30 new fighter jets at an expected cost of $1 billion to replace its older MiG-21 and MiG-23 fighters.

A Saab-British Aerospace Plc consortium is offering the JAS-39 Gripen while U.S. giants Lockheed Martin Corp. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., with the F-16C and F-18 respectively, are also seeking the deal along with France's Dassault Aviation, which builds Mirage jets.
Russia has also offered to sell Hungary MiG-29s and Su-39s, although NATO has warned that the Hungarian military must be "compatible" with alliance weaponry.
Cohen will visit Ukraine and Bulgaria later before flying home to Washington on Monday.

On another matter, Cohen on Wednesday defended a statement issued by summit leaders warning the former warring factions in Bosnia to comply with the Dayton peace accords, including demands that suspects indicted on charges of war crimes be turned over to the International Tribunal in the Hague.

But U.S. and NATO officials have declined comment on reports that they might change policy and allow their troops to arrest former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and others charged with war crimes.

"I thought the statement was pretty strongly worded and did reflect a strong sentiment by the NATO countries," said Cohen. He noted that U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Tuesday in Madrid that "Karadzic's day will come".
"Whether it comes earlier or later remains to be seen," Cohen said. "Let's wait and see what happens in the next several months."
